Al Jazeera: The Deir Yassin massacre: Why it still matters 75 years later
Algemeiner: Deir Yassin: The 'Massacre' That Never Was
Jewish Telegraphic Agency: Israelis, Palestinians dispute details of bloody 1948 assault
Spring Magazine: The legacy of the Deir Yassin Massacre
University of Arizona Center for Middle Eastern Studies: Document B, Deir Yassin Massacre (1948)
Middle East Forum: Deir Yassin: The End of the Myth (review of Eliezer Tauber's book)

content.p: On Friday 9 April 1948, fighters from the Irgun and the Lehi attacked Deir Yassin, a Palestinian Arab village on a hill west of Jerusalem. The Lehi was known to the British as the Stern Gang. The attack came about five weeks before Ben-Gurion proclaimed the state of Israel, while the British mandate was still running and Arab irregulars were besieging Jerusalem, according to Tablet. News of what happened there spread quickly, and Al Jazeera reports that thousands of Palestinians fled their villages in fear.

Almost eight decades later the event is still contested. Palestinians and their supporters have used the cry "Remember Deir Yassin" for decades, and the Jewish Telegraphic Agency noted in its report ahead of Israel's 50th anniversary that it had become a rallying call. Some Israeli historians and writers answer that the killings were the cost of a battle, and that the word "massacre" has been applied too readily. Sources disagree about how many people died, who ordered the attack, whether women were raped, and whether the killings continued after the fighting was over. The surviving accounts are set out below, each with the person or group that gives it.
content.h2: A village on the Jerusalem road
content.p: Deir Yassin sat about five kilometres from Jerusalem, on the road towards Jaffa. Its location mattered to everyone involved. Algemeiner says Operation Nachshon was meant to open the road to Jerusalem, where it says 100,000 Jews were trapped. A University of Arizona teaching document says the village lay outside the area the United Nations had assigned to a Jewish state, but on high ground in the corridor between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.

The village's size is also disputed. Al Jazeera says about 700 Palestinians lived there, mostly quarry workers and stonecutters. The University of Arizona document puts the population at about 750, and the Jewish Telegraphic Agency gives "some 500 Arabs". Al Jazeera adds that some Palestinians and Israeli historians describe a pact of non-aggression between the village and the Haganah. The Haganah intelligence officer Pa'il, quoted by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, described a similar understanding between the village head and the head of the nearby Jewish neighbourhood of Givat Shaul not to shoot at each other.

The two groups had long been rivals. The Irgun was founded in 1931 as the national military organisation, known by its Hebrew acronym Etzel. The Lehi split from it nine years after its founding. Tablet notes that the two groups united for this operation, hoping that taking Deir Yassin would break the siege of Jerusalem and let them fight as conventional soldiers rather than as guerrillas. Tablet adds that they had never before achieved the conquest of territory.

Sources differ on when the attack began: the Jewish Telegraphic Agency and Tablet say early in the morning, while Al Jazeera says it was a Friday afternoon. Accounts agree that the attackers meant to warn the villagers. Tablet, drawing on Tauber, says a loudspeaker vehicle was sent ahead to tell people to leave. The vehicle tumbled into a trench the villagers had dug, and the defenders' fire muffled the message. Algemeiner reports a view that some have held: the truck stuck in a ditch, mostly out of earshot of the village. Tablet describes house-to-house fighting. Algemeiner says the attackers expected to find only fighters, and did not allow for civilians still sheltering in the houses.

The Haganah's part is contested. Tauber, reviewed by the Middle East Forum, says the operation had the backing of David Shaltiel, the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander, and that the Haganah in Jerusalem supplied support and arms. The University of Arizona's teaching document says the Haganah authorised the Irgun and the Stern Gang to take the village. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency says the operation was carried out with help from the Haganah. Spring Magazine says the Haganah did not take part directly, but supplied aid and later took control of the village from the Irgun and Lehi.
Looting took place. Tablet, citing Tauber, says the Irgun and Lehi fighters looted the village and distributed much of the plunder to the besieged residents of Jerusalem.

A contemporary account comes from Jacques de Reynier, the representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Jerusalem. On 10 April the Arab Higher Committee asked him to help the wounded and recover the dead. He tried the Jewish Agency, which said it could do nothing because the attackers were Irgun extremists over whom it had no control. The British headquarters confirmed the troops' identity and said the fighting was over, but would not intervene. Through contacts he made overnight, he obtained Irgun permission to go to the village on the morning of 11 April, with two ambulances, two doctors and nurses from Magen David Adom, the Jewish equivalent of the Red Cross.

His memorandum to Geneva, dated 13 April, says that at the village he met an officer who told him there were no wounded, only about 200 dead. According to that officer, the attackers had warned the women and children to surrender at the start; 150 women and children gave themselves up and were sent to the British, and, according to the officer, the remainder were considered combatants and paid with their lives. The translation's annotator notes that de Reynier relied in part on second-hand information, much of it from Irgun or Lehi men, for details he did not see himself. The memorandum also records that he asked to see the dead and was taken to the centre of the village, where a new discussion began.

Al Jazeera and Spring Magazine both report a Red Cross representative's account of heaped bodies: some 150 in a cave and about 50 in a separate place. Spring says the 150 were Arab men, women and children, and places the 50 in a stronghold. Neither article gives the Red Cross text for that claim, so it should be read as their report of the Red Cross view.
The Jewish Telegraphic Agency calls the death toll perhaps the least controversial part of the debate, yet the figures still vary widely. They run in three groups.

The lowest comes from Tauber's name-by-name study, which Tablet describes as listing 101 dead villagers and estimating that about 100 more were injured, with 150 to 200 taken prisoner and then released. Tablet says 60 of the dead were men and 41 were women, some of whom had dressed as men and fought. Tauber concludes that 61 of 84 deaths whose circumstances he could establish happened under battle conditions. The Middle East Forum, which reviewed the book favourably, says Tauber found no more than 101 dead.

A middle group rests on Palestinian research. Algemeiner says the Arab researchers Sharif Kan'ane and Nihad Zeitawi compiled a list of 107 dead after interviewing survivors in 1987. Al Jazeera says at least 107 Palestinians were killed. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports that a study by Bir Zeit University found the fatalities did not exceed 120, and says at least 120 of the village's residents were killed.

The highest figures come from the period itself. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency says the original estimate was 240. A letter from the British delegation to the United Nations, quoted by Spring Magazine, says that "the deaths of some 250 Arabs" "took place in circumstances of great savagery". The Irgun commander told the Red Cross representative about 200. Tablet, which rejects the massacre account, still gives 254 as the figure for the story it disputes.
On the Jewish side, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports four soldiers killed. Tablet, citing Tauber, says about 120 Jewish soldiers took part and suffered 30 to 40 wounded, and that five died.
content.h2: Testimony and the question of rape
content.p: Historians disagree most sharply on what happened inside the houses. The Israeli historian Benny Morris, quoted by Al Jazeera, said the militias "ransacked unscrupulously, stole money and jewels from the survivors and burned the bodies. Even dismemberment and rape occurred." Al Jazeera also reports that the Jewish intellectual Martin Buber wrote at the time that "In Deir Yassin hundreds of innocent men, women and children were massacred."

Algemeiner, which argues that the massacre label is wrong, takes a different line. It says British police interviewed survivors who alleged rape, the cutting of pregnant women, and executions. It says Kan'ane and Zeitawi, interviewing survivors in 1987, found that not one testimony mentioned rape or mistreatment of women. Walid Khalidi, who used statements from 30 survivors, says, according to Algemeiner, that there were isolated killings of civilians, but that the allegations of rape and other extreme abuses were fabricated. Algemeiner adds, without naming a source for the claim, that the head of the Arab Higher Committee in Jerusalem persuaded survivors to repeat them.

Tauber, according to a Middle East Forum review, found no evidence for the rape accusations, and says that women and children died only when buildings where they had taken cover collapsed. Tablet, which reviews Tauber's book, says there is no credible evidence of systematic slaughter, rape or torture, and notes that there are no photographs.

The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports a claim from a Palestine Broadcasting Service editor, interviewed for a planned BBC series, that he had been told by the secretary of the Arab Higher Committee, Hussein Khalidi, to exaggerate abuses. A survivor, Radwan Abu-Mahmoud, told the BBC that the villagers had objected to being asked to exaggerate. These are accounts given decades later and are reported as such.

Some Jewish witnesses described the scene in strong terms. Mordechai Gichon, a Haganah intelligence officer sent to the village after the fighting, is quoted by Spring Magazine as saying "To me it looked a bit like a pogrom", and adding that his impression was "more of a massacre than anything else". Pa'il, another Haganah intelligence officer, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that he heard shooting from house to house and saw women, children and elderly men shot. He also said he saw some 25 men driven through Jerusalem and shot at an old quarry.

Pa'il's account of timing is disputed. The military historian Uri Milstein, who wrote a four-volume history of the 1948 war, contends, in the Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report, that most casualties happened during the fighting. Pa'il places the killings after the fighting ended, once the Haganah had pulled out and left Irgun and Lehi men in the village.

Menachem Begin led the Irgun, and Spring Magazine says Yitzhak Shamir led the Lehi during the 1948 war. Both later became prime ministers. Spring Magazine presents that career as evidence that no one involved was held to account. Algemeiner writes that Yehuda Segal was killed in the fighting for one house, and that another soldier then killed 11 members of the household whose occupants had surrendered. Algemeiner calls that a crime, and says it was not typical of Jewish soldiers.

The Israeli government's position shifted. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reports that Labor Zionist leaders first confirmed that a massacre had happened, possibly to discredit the Irgun and Lehi, and that the government later moved away from that view. In 1969 the then foreign minister, Abba Eban, issued a pamphlet calling the massacre accusation a "fairy tale" and "the 'big lie' of Deir Yassin". The pamphlet said that the Irgun "fought and won a battle", and that there was no aftermath of outrage or brutal excess.

The Haganah's own position in the village is also part of the record. Spring Magazine says a Jewish police officer sent to investigate on 14 April was not allowed beyond Givat Shaul by the Haganah, and that the Government of Palestine reported that it had not been able to enter the village.

News of the killings spread quickly. Al Jazeera says that, as it spread, thousands of Palestinians fled their villages in fear. The Israeli historian Benny Morris, quoted by Al Jazeera, said the village "had a profound demographic and political effect" and was "followed by mass flight of Arabs from their locales". Deir Yassin Remembered, a New York-based group that organised the anniversary campaign, says the attack marked the start of the depopulation of more than 400 Arab villages and the exile of roughly 700,000 Palestinians, as quoted by the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

Al Jazeera ties the attack to Plan Dalet, which the historian Ilan Pappé says Ben-Gurion authorised in March 1948, and says that Operation Nachshon was the first step of the plan. Al Jazeera names four nearby villages, Qalunya, Saris, Beit Surik and Biddu, as the four nearby villages that were next. Tauber's English subtitle ties the myth to the refugee question.
content.h2: An argument that has not ended
content.p: Tauber's 2017 Hebrew book, Deir Yassin: The End of the Myth, appeared in English as The Massacre That Never Was, with a subtitle that links the myth to the refugee question. Tablet reviewed it favourably and wrote that the book was being ignored. The Middle East Forum published a similar review. Tauber's position is that the fatalities were largely a consequence of battle, and that the rape and mutilation claims have no evidence behind them. Algemeiner shares that view and says the event is "invariably (and incorrectly) described as a 'massacre'".

Others reject that account. Al Jazeera presents Ilan Pappé's view that the attack was part of a planned strategy, Plan Dalet. Benny Morris, whose work Al Jazeera quotes, said the militias looted and burned bodies, and that "dismemberment and rape occurred". The Zionist Organization of America published a report titled "Deir Yassin: History of a Lie", which, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, says civilians were killed unintentionally during house-to-house fighting and that a Bir Zeit study put the toll at no more than 120. Daniel McGowan, director of Deir Yassin Remembered, called that report "revisionist propaganda".

What the sources share is a violent attack on a village of several hundred people, in which civilians were among the dead; Tablet says too many noncombatants were killed. The counts range from 101 to about 250, depending on whose list is used. Some survivors' accounts were recorded by the British soon after the event, and others have since been challenged. Whether the killings were a battle, a massacre, or both, remains a question each reader must weigh against the sources.
